title: Single-Dose Psychedelic Nasal Spray Eases Treatment-Resistant Depression in JAMA Trial
excerpt: In a 193-person phase 2b trial, one intranasal dose of mebufotenin cut depression scores by 5.3 points more than a near-zero control dose at four weeks — with the psychedelic effect over in about an hour.
body:
• A single nasal-spray dose of mebufotenin, a short-acting psychedelic, significantly reduced symptoms in 193 adults with treatment-resistant depression, in a phase 2b trial published in JAMA on October 26.
  • At day 29, the 12 mg dose beat a 0.3 mg low-dose control by 5.3 points on the 60-point MADRS depression scale; about one-third of patients on active doses saw scores fall by at least half.
  • Remission reached 18-26% on active doses versus 8% on the control — an absolute gain of roughly 10-18 percentage points.
  • The drug is not approved anywhere; the trial was funded by its developer, Beckley Psytech, and larger, longer trials are still needed.

A single dose of a fast-acting psychedelic nasal spray produced rapid and lasting improvement in people whose depression had resisted multiple standard treatments, according to a clinical trial published in JAMA this week. The drug, mebufotenin benzoate (BPL-003), is a synthetic formulation of 5-MeO-DMT, a psychedelic whose effects peak within 8 to 15 minutes and fade within about an hour.

What the trial did

The randomized, double-blind phase 2b trial enrolled 193 adults aged 18 to 75 across 38 sites in Australia, Europe and the United States between September 2023 and April 2025. Every participant had treatment-resistant depression, having already tried between two and five antidepressant treatments without success. Participants received a single intranasal dose of 8 mg or 12 mg of mebufotenin, or a 0.3 mg sub-perceptual dose as the comparator. Neither participants, clinic staff nor the researchers rating symptoms knew who received what.

The results, in absolute terms

The primary outcome was change on the Montgomery-Åsberg Depression Rating Scale (MADRS), a 60-point clinician-rated scale, at day 29. The 12 mg dose outperformed the low-dose control by a mean of 5.3 points — a statistically significant difference. Roughly one-third of participants on either higher dose saw their symptom scores fall by at least half, and remission was reported in 18-26% of treated patients compared with 8% on the control dose. In plain terms, for every 100 people treated, roughly 10 to 18 more reached remission than would have on the near-inactive dose. Benefits emerged one day after dosing and were largely maintained to eight weeks, Medical Xpress reported.

The practical difference from other psychedelic therapies is time. Psilocybin sessions can require 4 to 12 hours of monitoring. Here, 85% of participants in the 8 mg group and 78% in the 12 mg group met all safety criteria and were ready for discharge within two hours of dosing.

Caveats before anyone gets excited

Side effects were mostly mild or moderate and occurred mainly on the dosing day, including nausea, anxiety and panic. But this was a single-dose, sponsor-funded trial: Beckley Psytech, an AtaiBeckley company developing the drug, paid for the study. The researchers themselves note that future studies with longer observation are needed to establish how long benefits last and whether repeat dosing is required. Treatment-resistant depression affects roughly 30% of people diagnosed with major depression, and existing alternatives — ketamine-based treatments and magnetic brain stimulation — demand frequent clinic visits. A confirmed one-visit option would be a genuine change in that landscape, but confirmation is exactly what has not happened yet. Anyone with depression that has not responded to treatment should discuss options with their psychiatrist rather than seeking psychedelics outside a regulated trial.
